top_news.title: Indian Medical Parliamentarians
top_news.summary: VMPL Vapi (Gujarat) [India], September 23: The Indian Medical Parliamentarians' Forum (IMPF) convened the National Policy Summit on MedTech Access on September 22 at Meril Academy, Vapi, under the theme "Swasth Bharat Se Saksham Bharat | Reimagining MedTech Access in India." The summit brought together Members of Parliament, senior government officials, healthcare institutions, clinical experts and industry stakeholders to deliberate on strengthening India's medical technology ecosystem and expanding access to quality, advanced and affordable healthcare technologies. The summit was chaired by Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha and Chairperson, IMPF. Senior representatives from the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Department of Health Research, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Health Authority (NHA), AIIMS Nagpur and the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC) participated in the discussions. The summit featured two panel discussions that brought together policymakers, healthcare experts, academic leaders and industry representatives to advance reform-oriented discussions on India's medical technology ecosystem and pathways to wider patient access. The first panel, "Building a Sustainable and Globally Competitive MedTech Ecosystem," examined the enabling ecosystem required to support indigenous medical technology development and global competitiveness. The discussion covered areas including research and innovation, regulatory and quality frameworks, industry-academia collaboration, domestic manufacturing capabilities, supply-chain resilience, clinical requirements and the creation of an ecosystem that could support Indian MedTech companies in addressing both domestic and global healthcare needs. The panel was chaired by Dr Shivaji Bandappa Kalge, with Shri Manoj Joshi serving as Co-Chair. Dr Vibhav Garg, Moderator, Meril, moderated the discussion, which also featured Prof. (Dr.) Prashant P. Joshi and Dr Neha Dumka as panellists. The second panel, "Expanding Access to Quality Care through MedTech Innovation," focused on the factors that determine whether medical technology can translate from innovation into meaningful patient access. The discussion examined clinical evidence, health technology assessment, financing and reimbursement, technology adoption, healthcare workforce capabilities and the challenges of extending advanced technologies across different levels of the health system. The panel was chaired by Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar and moderated by Dr Sharmila Sarkar, with Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan, Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav and Dr Suchita Markan participating as panellists. Speaking at the summit, Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha and Chairperson, IMPF, said, "Innovation without access has limited impact, and access without evidence cannot be sustained. For India to build a globally competitive medical technology ecosystem, we need stronger indigenous research and development, credible clinical evidence, appropriate health technology assessment and sustainable reimbursement mechanisms. Manufacturing must be supported by the right clinical skills, infrastructure and technical ecosystem, particularly as advanced technologies such as robotics become more accessible. Our ultimate objective must be Indian innovation, global-quality technology and affordable access for every patient who needs it." Shri Manoj Kumar Joshi, Co-Chair and Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, said, "For India to become self-reliant in medical devices, we need a strong ecosystem built around quality, evidence and credibility. Our regulatory system must evolve to ensure that products developed in India meet globally credible standards. At the same time, we need to strengthen domestic supply chains, engineering capabilities and component manufacturing. Building this ecosystem will not only support healthcare access but also contribute to employment and the country's overall prosperity." Addressing the role of healthcare institutions in advancing medical technology, Dr Prashant P. Joshi said, "Medical institutions should not be limited to validating technologies developed elsewhere; they should help identify unmet clinical needs and work with engineers, researchers and innovators to develop solutions around those needs. We need stronger collaboration between medical and engineering institutions through joint research, academic programmes, fellowships and training. At AIIMS Nagpur, we are exploring such collaborations with institutions such as IIT Bombay. Building this interdisciplinary ecosystem can significantly strengthen India's medical technology innovation and ultimately improve patient care." Highlighting the importance of clinical adoption and capacity building, Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan said, "Access to medical technology is not simply about making a device available. A device can create meaningful impact only when healthcare professionals are able to use it safely, confidently and effectively. We need to move from an equipment-centric approach to a technology adoption model, with competency-based training for clinicians, technicians and other healthcare professionals. Digital learning and remote training can also help extend this capacity to underserved and rural areas." Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav, IAS, Joint Director, National Health Authority, highlighted the importance of linking innovation with sustainable financing and reimbursement. He said, "For a medical technology to reach the patient, clinical effectiveness must be supported by appropriate financing and reimbursement pathways. Under Ayushman Bharat, newer interventions require credible clinical and economic evidence before they can be incorporated into health benefit packages. We also need to look beyond the upfront cost of a device and consider the total cost of care, including treatment, hospitalisation, personnel and follow-up. This will help us build a healthcare system that is both affordable and sustainable." Emphasising the need to evaluate technologies within the realities of the health system, Dr Neha Dumka said, "Technology has an important role to play in strengthening primary healthcare, particularly as our disease burden continues to evolve. However, innovation must be assessed not only for its technical capabilities, but also for ease of use, cost-effectiveness, scalability and sustainability within the health system. We need to ensure that technologies can be effectively adopted at different levels of care and ultimately reach the beneficiaries who need them. Strengthening this pathway will be essential for equitable access to quality healthcare." Speaking on strengthening healthcare delivery at the grassroots, Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar said, "To take medical technology from innovation to meaningful patient access, we first need to identify the bottlenecks in the existing system. We must strengthen the capabilities of healthcare professionals at the grassroots, particularly those working at CHCs and sub-district centres. Technologies should be introduced systematically and evaluated through comparative, data-based studies. Most importantly, their acceptability among healthcare professionals and patients must be considered if we want innovations to achieve meaningful adoption." Highlighting the potential of Indian medical device manufacturers, Dr Shivaji Kalge said, "Indian medical device companies are increasingly capable of developing technologies that meet international standards while remaining affordable for Indian patients. We are already seeing Indian companies compete with international products in areas such as ophthalmology and other medical specialties. If we continue to strengthen research, quality and innovation, these technologies can become more widely accepted globally. This can help improve access to quality healthcare for Indian patients at more affordable prices." The summit brought together senior government and institutional leaders from across India's healthcare ecosystem, including Shri Manoj Kumar Joshi, Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, who served as Co-Chair. The summit also featured Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha, Maharashtra. The gathering further included senior representatives from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), National Health Authority (NHA), leading government medical institutions, clinical experts and key industry associations. The discussions at the summit underscored the need for a coordinated approach spanning indigenous innovation, evidence generation, regulatory quality, clinical education, health technology assessment, financing, reimbursement and institutional adoption. The deliberations also highlighted the importance of connecting medical technology innovation with the needs of healthcare providers and patients, particularly in underserved areas. About the Indian Medical Parliamentarians Forum (IMPF) Established in 2006, the IMPF is a non-partisan platform for Members of Parliament from both Houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) who have backgrounds in medicine and healthcare. The forum fosters evidence-based dialogue on public health priorities and connects parliamentary leadership with the government, clinical experts, civil society, academia and the industry, enabling the formulation of national policies grounded in the realities of healthcare on the ground. top_news.title: Minister’s eye ‘absolutely on ball’ as figures show surge in drug deaths - AOL
top_news.summary: Scotland’s drug and alcohol minister has insisted her “eye is absolutely on the ball” after the number of drugs deaths in the country surged to 1,133. Deaths from illicit drug use in Scotland rose by 11% last year and remains by far the highest rate in Europe. Maree Todd said the Government must “work harder and faster” to stem the rise amid the flood of powerful synthetic drugs. The minister, who took up the role in June 2025, said it was “impossible” to say whether she was doing a good job “on a day like today when we’re facing statistics like this”, which showed 116 more people had died than in 2024. The figures from the National Records of Scotland (NRS) show the rate of deaths from drug poisoning were 2.4 times higher than it was in England, 1.6 times greater than in Northern Ireland and 1.5 times more than in Wales – with these figures covering 2024, the most recent year for which data is available for all parts of the UK. Nitazenes – synthetic opioids – were implicated in 247 drug use deaths in 2025, with Etonitazene, the most common nitazene, being involved in 215 drug use deaths. Drugs deaths were down by 5% for women but skyrocketed by 19% for men. More than one drug was implicated in 78% of deaths, with the figures also showing a 23% rise in deaths where cocaine was implicated, the highest on record. Speaking to the Press Association in Glasgow , Ms Todd said: “My heartfelt condolences go out to each and every family that has experienced loss. “These figures are devastating, these deaths are preventable, and behind each and every number is a family who are feeling loss.” She said: “It’s really painful that what we’ve seen is a rise in drugs deaths in 2025 compared to the year before. I would have hoped, with all of the work that we are doing across the system, we wouldn’t be facing that situation.” “We’ve seen a rise in synthetic opioids that are exceptionally potent and causing death and destruction on our streets,” she added. Ms Todd said experts had told her the Scottish Government was taking “all the right steps” to tackle drug deaths. Asked about former first minister Nicola Sturgeon’s admission in 2021 that the Government took its “eye off the ball”, Ms Todd told PA: “My eye is absolutely on the ball.” But she admitted there was “absolutely no getting away from how painful it is to be standing here in front of you today and looking at a rise in drugs deaths”, adding that she would not “shy away from responsibility”. The drugs minister said there should be “no reason” why people with addiction should struggle to access rehab, saying cash had been given to councils and that “money should be no object”. Promising action, she added: “What I absolutely commit to do to you and to all of the people who are listening or watching, is to redouble my efforts to keep working on all of the things that I know will make a difference right across the suite of our efforts, and we will make progress.” Catriona Matheson, professor in substance use at the University of Stirling, said “highly potent synthetic opioids” were contaminating heroin and other opioids, posing a “serious risk” to drug users. “We are also still seeing high levels of cocaine use alongside other substances, fuelled by the availability of low-cost cocaine through international drug markets,” she said. “While the drivers of supply are often beyond Scotland’s control, their impact is being felt in communities across the country.” Jackie Baillie, Scottish Labour’s health spokeswoman, said despite ministers declaring a drugs emergency years ago, “it is shameful that things are still moving in the wrong direction”. She said: “This is a damning indictment of the Scottish Government’s failure to support some of the most marginalised people in Scotland. “Action is long overdue and we cannot afford any more delays while lives are being lost.” The Scottish Greens warned the SNP it “cannot keep repeating the same failed approach and expect different results”. Health spokesperson Kayleigh Kinross-O’Neill said ministers could not cut the number of drug deaths “without tackling the conditions that are driving harmful drug use in the first place, such as poverty, trauma, poor mental health, isolation, and deprivation”. Reform MSP Victor Currie said: “Today’s figures land less than 24 hours after yesterday’s homelessness statistics delivered the other half of the one-two punch – a surge in homeless children, rough sleeping and families stuck in temporary accommodation. “Together they reveal a government that has locked Scotland into a doom spiral, where one form of social collapse only feeds the next.” The Scottish Drugs Forum called for more safer drug consumption facilities and drug checking services. Chief executive Kirsten Horsburgh added: “It is too simplistic to say that 1,133 people died because of the contaminated drug supply, or indeed because of drug use itself. The truth is that these deaths are shaped by a much wider set of factors, including poverty, trauma, deprivation, housing insecurity and mental health inequality.” Drug deaths are 15 times higher in Scotland’s most deprived communities, with the average age of death increasing from 32 in 2000 to 46 in 2025. Scottish Liberal Democrat leader Alex Cole Hamilton said: “There is no shortage of powers that the Scottish Government has at its disposal to end this crisis and stop people dying. This loss of life must compel them to finally make the most of those powers and deliver the world-class drug services Scotland deserves.” Conservative MSP Miles Briggs said the “horrific figures” showed the SNP’s approach has “catastrophically failed”. “They cannot continue to double down on their policies when the number of lives being lost has soared over the last year. They must shut down their flagship Thistle facility in Glasgow and ditch any plans for more state-sponsored drug taking at drug consumption rooms, including in Edinburgh,” he said. articles.title: Indian Medical Parliamentarians
articles.summary: VMPL Vapi (Gujarat) [India], September 23: The Indian Medical Parliamentarians' Forum (IMPF) convened the National Policy Summit on MedTech Access on September 22 at Meril Academy, Vapi, under the theme "Swasth Bharat Se Saksham Bharat | Reimagining MedTech Access in India." The summit brought together Members of Parliament, senior government officials, healthcare institutions, clinical experts and industry stakeholders to deliberate on strengthening India's medical technology ecosystem and expanding access to quality, advanced and affordable healthcare technologies. The summit was chaired by Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha and Chairperson, IMPF. Senior representatives from the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Department of Health Research, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Health Authority (NHA), AIIMS Nagpur and the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC) participated in the discussions. The summit featured two panel discussions that brought together policymakers, healthcare experts, academic leaders and industry representatives to advance reform-oriented discussions on India's medical technology ecosystem and pathways to wider patient access. The first panel, "Building a Sustainable and Globally Competitive MedTech Ecosystem," examined the enabling ecosystem required to support indigenous medical technology development and global competitiveness. The discussion covered areas including research and innovation, regulatory and quality frameworks, industry-academia collaboration, domestic manufacturing capabilities, supply-chain resilience, clinical requirements and the creation of an ecosystem that could support Indian MedTech companies in addressing both domestic and global healthcare needs. The panel was chaired by Dr Shivaji Bandappa Kalge, with Shri Manoj Joshi serving as Co-Chair. Dr Vibhav Garg, Moderator, Meril, moderated the discussion, which also featured Prof. (Dr.) Prashant P. Joshi and Dr Neha Dumka as panellists. The second panel, "Expanding Access to Quality Care through MedTech Innovation," focused on the factors that determine whether medical technology can translate from innovation into meaningful patient access. The discussion examined clinical evidence, health technology assessment, financing and reimbursement, technology adoption, healthcare workforce capabilities and the challenges of extending advanced technologies across different levels of the health system. The panel was chaired by Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar and moderated by Dr Sharmila Sarkar, with Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan, Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav and Dr Suchita Markan participating as panellists. Speaking at the summit, Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha and Chairperson, IMPF, said, "Innovation without access has limited impact, and access without evidence cannot be sustained. For India to build a globally competitive medical technology ecosystem, we need stronger indigenous research and development, credible clinical evidence, appropriate health technology assessment and sustainable reimbursement mechanisms. Manufacturing must be supported by the right clinical skills, infrastructure and technical ecosystem, particularly as advanced technologies such as robotics become more accessible. Our ultimate objective must be Indian innovation, global-quality technology and affordable access for every patient who needs it." Shri Manoj Kumar Joshi, Co-Chair and Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, said, "For India to become self-reliant in medical devices, we need a strong ecosystem built around quality, evidence and credibility. Our regulatory system must evolve to ensure that products developed in India meet globally credible standards. At the same time, we need to strengthen domestic supply chains, engineering capabilities and component manufacturing. Building this ecosystem will not only support healthcare access but also contribute to employment and the country's overall prosperity." Addressing the role of healthcare institutions in advancing medical technology, Dr Prashant P. Joshi said, "Medical institutions should not be limited to validating technologies developed elsewhere; they should help identify unmet clinical needs and work with engineers, researchers and innovators to develop solutions around those needs. We need stronger collaboration between medical and engineering institutions through joint research, academic programmes, fellowships and training. At AIIMS Nagpur, we are exploring such collaborations with institutions such as IIT Bombay. Building this interdisciplinary ecosystem can significantly strengthen India's medical technology innovation and ultimately improve patient care." Highlighting the importance of clinical adoption and capacity building, Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan said, "Access to medical technology is not simply about making a device available. A device can create meaningful impact only when healthcare professionals are able to use it safely, confidently and effectively. We need to move from an equipment-centric approach to a technology adoption model, with competency-based training for clinicians, technicians and other healthcare professionals. Digital learning and remote training can also help extend this capacity to underserved and rural areas." Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav, IAS, Joint Director, National Health Authority, highlighted the importance of linking innovation with sustainable financing and reimbursement. He said, "For a medical technology to reach the patient, clinical effectiveness must be supported by appropriate financing and reimbursement pathways. Under Ayushman Bharat, newer interventions require credible clinical and economic evidence before they can be incorporated into health benefit packages. We also need to look beyond the upfront cost of a device and consider the total cost of care, including treatment, hospitalisation, personnel and follow-up. This will help us build a healthcare system that is both affordable and sustainable." Emphasising the need to evaluate technologies within the realities of the health system, Dr Neha Dumka said, "Technology has an important role to play in strengthening primary healthcare, particularly as our disease burden continues to evolve. However, innovation must be assessed not only for its technical capabilities, but also for ease of use, cost-effectiveness, scalability and sustainability within the health system. We need to ensure that technologies can be effectively adopted at different levels of care and ultimately reach the beneficiaries who need them. Strengthening this pathway will be essential for equitable access to quality healthcare." Speaking on strengthening healthcare delivery at the grassroots, Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar said, "To take medical technology from innovation to meaningful patient access, we first need to identify the bottlenecks in the existing system. We must strengthen the capabilities of healthcare professionals at the grassroots, particularly those working at CHCs and sub-district centres. Technologies should be introduced systematically and evaluated through comparative, data-based studies. Most importantly, their acceptability among healthcare professionals and patients must be considered if we want innovations to achieve meaningful adoption." Highlighting the potential of Indian medical device manufacturers, Dr Shivaji Kalge said, "Indian medical device companies are increasingly capable of developing technologies that meet international standards while remaining affordable for Indian patients. We are already seeing Indian companies compete with international products in areas such as ophthalmology and other medical specialties. If we continue to strengthen research, quality and innovation, these technologies can become more widely accepted globally. This can help improve access to quality healthcare for Indian patients at more affordable prices." The summit brought together senior government and institutional leaders from across India's healthcare ecosystem, including Shri Manoj Kumar Joshi, Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, who served as Co-Chair. The summit also featured Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha, Maharashtra. The gathering further included senior representatives from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), National Health Authority (NHA), leading government medical institutions, clinical experts and key industry associations. The discussions at the summit underscored the need for a coordinated approach spanning indigenous innovation, evidence generation, regulatory quality, clinical education, health technology assessment, financing, reimbursement and institutional adoption. The deliberations also highlighted the importance of connecting medical technology innovation with the needs of healthcare providers and patients, particularly in underserved areas. About the Indian Medical Parliamentarians Forum (IMPF) Established in 2006, the IMPF is a non-partisan platform for Members of Parliament from both Houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) who have backgrounds in medicine and healthcare. The forum fosters evidence-based dialogue on public health priorities and connects parliamentary leadership with the government, clinical experts, civil society, academia and the industry, enabling the formulation of national policies grounded in the realities of healthcare on the ground. articles.title: Minister’s eye ‘absolutely on ball’ as figures show surge in drug deaths - AOL
articles.summary: Scotland’s drug and alcohol minister has insisted her “eye is absolutely on the ball” after the number of drugs deaths in the country surged to 1,133. Deaths from illicit drug use in Scotland rose by 11% last year and remains by far the highest rate in Europe. Maree Todd said the Government must “work harder and faster” to stem the rise amid the flood of powerful synthetic drugs. The minister, who took up the role in June 2025, said it was “impossible” to say whether she was doing a good job “on a day like today when we’re facing statistics like this”, which showed 116 more people had died than in 2024. The figures from the National Records of Scotland (NRS) show the rate of deaths from drug poisoning were 2.4 times higher than it was in England, 1.6 times greater than in Northern Ireland and 1.5 times more than in Wales – with these figures covering 2024, the most recent year for which data is available for all parts of the UK. Nitazenes – synthetic opioids – were implicated in 247 drug use deaths in 2025, with Etonitazene, the most common nitazene, being involved in 215 drug use deaths. Drugs deaths were down by 5% for women but skyrocketed by 19% for men. More than one drug was implicated in 78% of deaths, with the figures also showing a 23% rise in deaths where cocaine was implicated, the highest on record. Speaking to the Press Association in Glasgow , Ms Todd said: “My heartfelt condolences go out to each and every family that has experienced loss. “These figures are devastating, these deaths are preventable, and behind each and every number is a family who are feeling loss.” She said: “It’s really painful that what we’ve seen is a rise in drugs deaths in 2025 compared to the year before. I would have hoped, with all of the work that we are doing across the system, we wouldn’t be facing that situation.” “We’ve seen a rise in synthetic opioids that are exceptionally potent and causing death and destruction on our streets,” she added. Ms Todd said experts had told her the Scottish Government was taking “all the right steps” to tackle drug deaths. Asked about former first minister Nicola Sturgeon’s admission in 2021 that the Government took its “eye off the ball”, Ms Todd told PA: “My eye is absolutely on the ball.” But she admitted there was “absolutely no getting away from how painful it is to be standing here in front of you today and looking at a rise in drugs deaths”, adding that she would not “shy away from responsibility”. The drugs minister said there should be “no reason” why people with addiction should struggle to access rehab, saying cash had been given to councils and that “money should be no object”. Promising action, she added: “What I absolutely commit to do to you and to all of the people who are listening or watching, is to redouble my efforts to keep working on all of the things that I know will make a difference right across the suite of our efforts, and we will make progress.” Catriona Matheson, professor in substance use at the University of Stirling, said “highly potent synthetic opioids” were contaminating heroin and other opioids, posing a “serious risk” to drug users. “We are also still seeing high levels of cocaine use alongside other substances, fuelled by the availability of low-cost cocaine through international drug markets,” she said. “While the drivers of supply are often beyond Scotland’s control, their impact is being felt in communities across the country.” Jackie Baillie, Scottish Labour’s health spokeswoman, said despite ministers declaring a drugs emergency years ago, “it is shameful that things are still moving in the wrong direction”. She said: “This is a damning indictment of the Scottish Government’s failure to support some of the most marginalised people in Scotland. “Action is long overdue and we cannot afford any more delays while lives are being lost.” The Scottish Greens warned the SNP it “cannot keep repeating the same failed approach and expect different results”. Health spokesperson Kayleigh Kinross-O’Neill said ministers could not cut the number of drug deaths “without tackling the conditions that are driving harmful drug use in the first place, such as poverty, trauma, poor mental health, isolation, and deprivation”. Reform MSP Victor Currie said: “Today’s figures land less than 24 hours after yesterday’s homelessness statistics delivered the other half of the one-two punch – a surge in homeless children, rough sleeping and families stuck in temporary accommodation. “Together they reveal a government that has locked Scotland into a doom spiral, where one form of social collapse only feeds the next.” The Scottish Drugs Forum called for more safer drug consumption facilities and drug checking services. Chief executive Kirsten Horsburgh added: “It is too simplistic to say that 1,133 people died because of the contaminated drug supply, or indeed because of drug use itself. The truth is that these deaths are shaped by a much wider set of factors, including poverty, trauma, deprivation, housing insecurity and mental health inequality.” Drug deaths are 15 times higher in Scotland’s most deprived communities, with the average age of death increasing from 32 in 2000 to 46 in 2025. Scottish Liberal Democrat leader Alex Cole Hamilton said: “There is no shortage of powers that the Scottish Government has at its disposal to end this crisis and stop people dying. This loss of life must compel them to finally make the most of those powers and deliver the world-class drug services Scotland deserves.” Conservative MSP Miles Briggs said the “horrific figures” showed the SNP’s approach has “catastrophically failed”. “They cannot continue to double down on their policies when the number of lives being lost has soared over the last year. They must shut down their flagship Thistle facility in Glasgow and ditch any plans for more state-sponsored drug taking at drug consumption rooms, including in Edinburgh,” he said.
